title: King and pawn against king
summary: The square, the king in front, the opposition and the diagonal from both sides, the seventh rank without check and the corner: the door to pawn endings.
part.square.title: The square of the pawn
part.square.summary: Does the pawn run on its own? Count the square; a pawn on the second rank counts from the third.
part.opposition.title: King in front and the opposition
part.opposition.summary: When the black king catches the pawn, my king goes in front, and whoever moves gives way.
step.t_square: Your king is far away and the black king is chasing the pawn. Does it arrive in time, or does the pawn queen on its own?
step.t_square.hint1: Draw a square with one side running from the pawn to its queening square. Can the black king step into it?
step.intro: One extra pawn and the two kings: almost every pawn ending comes down to this, and knowing at a glance whether it wins or draws is worth a lot of points. Today we ask the questions that decide. Can the black king catch the pawn? Can my king get in front of it, and by which road? Who has the opposition? When may the pawn go to the seventh? And, for the defender, where is the corner or the stalemate that saves the game?
step.square: First question: can the king catch the pawn on its own? Don't calculate; draw. Run the diagonal from the pawn to the last rank and close the square: here, from g4 to c8. If the black king steps into the square, it catches the pawn. The king on b6 is outside, and it is my move: the pawn runs.
step.squareMove: White to play and win. Run with the pawn and watch the square shrink each move, always one step ahead of the black king.
step.squareMove.hint: Only the pawn. A king move gives the black king the time to step into the square.
step.squareMove.done: A new queen. The black king chased a square that shrank faster than it could walk.
step.t_opposition: The kings face each other, with yours in front of the pawn. Where can the black king go, and how does your king get past it in each case?
step.t_opposition.hint1: When one king must step aside, the other one advances. See which square your king gains.
step.front: In part 1 the pawn ran on its own. When the black king catches up, my king has to clear the road, and it goes in front of the pawn, not behind it: Averbakh said the king leads the pawn the way a father leads his child across the street. Here the kings face each other with one square between them: that is the opposition. Whoever has to move gives way.
step.opposition: White to play and win. The black king guards the squares in front of yours. Take the opposition and, when it gives way, walk past it.
step.opposition.hint: Put your king face to face with the black king, one square between them. The pawn waits.
step.opposition.done: That's it. Your king got in front of the pawn with the opposition, and the black king can no longer hold. The key squares lesson takes this road all the way.
step.recap: Six rules to take with you. One: the king catches the pawn if it gets into the square; a pawn on the second rank counts from the third. Two: the king goes in front of the pawn, and in the opposition whoever moves gives way. Three: a king that is far away comes back along the diagonal, yours or your opponent's; count both kings' moves. Four: the defender takes the opposition and stays in front of the pawn, stepping straight back. Five: with the king on the sixth, the pawn goes to the seventh without check. Six: in the corner, stalemate saves the defender. Here, for example, 1.g3 or 1.g4 only draws: the black king is inside the square. King first.
step.finish: Now play until you queen. The black king is already in front of the pawn: my king comes first.
ex.e13: White to play and win. The knight pawn is on the sixth rank, and the black king has hidden in the corner. Beware of the move that looks strongest.
ex.e13.hint: Before each move, count the black king's squares. If it has none and is not in check, it is stalemate.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Kc6! and, after 1...Kb8, 2.b7! After 2...Ka7, 3.Kc7 and the pawn queens. 1.Kc7?? seems to trap the black king, but it is stalemate: no square and no check. 1.b7+? gives the pawn away: 1...Kxb7. With a knight pawn and the black king in the corner, always count its squares.
ex.e14: White to play and draw. The black king stands beside the pawn, and yours is still behind. A position from the Encyclopedia of Chess Endings (Matanović, 1982), colours reversed.
ex.e14.hint: Your king wants to stand in front of the pawn, not beside it. And when the pawn advances, step straight back.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Kd2!, in front of the pawn. After 1...d3, 2.Kd1!, stepping back on the same file; after 2...Ke3, 3.Ke1!, face to face with the black king; after 3...d2+, 4.Kd1. Now the black king either abandons the pawn or goes to d3, and you are stalemated. 1.Ke1? or 1.Kd1? on the first move lose: the black king takes the front with 1...Ke3 or 1...Kd3. 2.Kc1? on the second move loses too.
ex.e11: Black to play and draw. The natural move loses.
ex.e11.hint: Don't think about the square in front of the pawn; think about the white king. Stand face to face with it.
ex.e11.solution: 1...Ke6!, the opposition: the white king can't climb through d5, e5 or f5. 1...Kd6? looks natural, but 2.Kd4! takes the opposition and the white king gets through.
key.square: The rule of the square: the black king is outside the pawn's square and can no longer catch it. The pawn runs on its own and promotes.
key.opposition: Kings face to face with one square between them: whoever has to move must give way. Here Black is to move, and the white king goes forward.
key.fishbein: The black king seems to catch the pawn, but the white king steps into its path and acts as a shield. The pawn promotes.
key.rookPawn: Rook pawn with the black king in the corner: a draw, whoever moves. The white king can't drive it out without stalemating it.
history: King and pawn against king is the first pawn ending every player needs to know, because almost every pawn ending ends up there. It looks simple, but it isn't: with the same extra pawn, one square more or less for the king decides between a win and a draw, and the edge pawn, the rook pawn, nearly always draws. Yuri Averbakh, a great endgame scholar, used to say the king leads the pawn the way a father walks his child across the street: in front. Even the best depend on it: in Zurich, in 1959, the Hungarian Gedeon Barcza saved a draw against Bobby Fischer because his king reached the corner in time, in front of the rook pawn.
practice: Now the real ending: king on d2, pawn on g2, and the black king inside the square. King first, then the pawn. Pick your time control and go.
ex.e15: White to play and win. Your king has gone too far, and the black king is close to the pawn. Which way back?
ex.e15.hint: First: does the pawn run alone, or is the black king inside the square? Then count your king's moves to the front of the pawn. The diagonal is as fast as the straight line.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Ke6!, 2.Kd5! and 3.Kc4! Along the diagonal the white king reaches c4, in front of the pawn, before the black king, and from there the pawn walks up protected. 1.b4? or 1.b3? don't work: the black king is inside the square and catches the pawn. 1.Ke7? or 1.Kf6? seem to head back, but they get no closer to c4, and the black king gains the tempo it needs.
ex.e16: White to play and win. The pawn is on the sixth rank, but the black king is coming and yours is far away. Calculate the race to the end.
ex.e16.hint: The white king must get next to the pawn before the black king stops in front of it. And the pawn goes to the seventh only when it does not give check.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Kb5! and 2.Kc6! The only road that arrives in time; 1.Ka5? or 1.Kb4? are a move behind, and 1.d7? at once only draws: 1...Ke7 picks up the pawn. After 2...Kd8, 3.d7!, without check; after 3...Ke7, 4.Kc7 and the pawn queens. 2.d7+? one move earlier, with the black king on e8, draws: 2...Kd8, and the black king stays in front of the pawn.
ex.e17: Black to play and draw. The white king is coming to help the knight pawn, and your king is far away. Only one road saves you, and the end hides one more trap.
ex.e17.hint: Run along the diagonal towards the squares in front of the pawn. At the end, remember: with a knight pawn, the corner can be the best place, because of stalemate.
ex.e17.solution: 1...Ke5!, 2...Kd6!, 3...Kc7! and 4...Kb7! Along the diagonal the black king gets in front of the pawn in time; 1...Kf5? or 1...Ke4? arrive a move late. After 5.b6, 5...Kb8!, and after 6.Ka6, 6...Ka8! Now if 7.b7+, 7...Kb8, and the white king can only protect the pawn with 8.Kb6, which is stalemate. 6...Kc8? on the last move loses: 7.Ka7 and the pawn queens.
part.diagonal.title: The king's road: the diagonal
part.diagonal.summary: A king far from the pawn comes back along the diagonal, as fast as along the straight line.
part.defendOpposition.title: The defender takes the opposition too
part.defendOpposition.summary: As Black, stand face to face with the white king; stepping back hands over the opposition.
part.defendFront.title: In front of the pawn
part.defendFront.summary: Matanović's defence: in front, straight back, face to face with the king, and stalemate.
part.seventh.title: The seventh rank without check
part.seventh.summary: With the king on the sixth, the pawn goes to the seventh without check; the check leads to stalemate.
part.corners.title: The corner: rook pawn and knight pawn
part.corners.summary: Barcza against Fischer, the corner that saves, and the rules to take with you.
step.t_square.hint2: From the pawn on g4 to g8 is four squares. Count four files towards the black king.
step.d_doubleStep: Now the pawn on the second rank. It may move two squares on its first move, so you count the square as if it already stood on the third: from b3 to g8. The king on h5 is outside.
step.d_doubleStep.m1: 1.b4!, the double step. The square now runs from b4 to f8, and the black king cannot reach the f-file in time. With 1.b3?, the square would run from b3 to g8, and 1...Kg6 would step into it.
step.d_doubleStep.m2: The king runs along the diagonal, the shortest road to the pawn.
step.d_doubleStep.m3: The square shrinks: from b5 to e8. To get in, the king would have to be on the e-file, and it is on the g-file.
step.d_doubleStep.m4: One more step along the diagonal, and still outside the square.
step.d_doubleStep.m5: Now the square runs from b6 to d8. The king on f7 is two files away from it.
step.d_doubleStep.m6: Too late: the pawn is two steps from queening.
step.d_doubleStep.m7: The black king can reach d7 or d8, but not b8. Next move the pawn queens.
step.t_opposition.hint2: If it leaves on the d side, your king goes past on the b side, and vice versa.
step.d_opposition: Black is to move and has to step aside. Watch my king walk through. If it were my move, I would be the one giving way, and the ending would be a draw.
step.d_opposition.m1: The black king has to step aside and picks the d side; that leaves b6 free for my king.
step.d_opposition.m2: 2.Kb6! I go past on the side it left. 2.Kb5 and 2.Kd5 also win; stepping back with 2.Kb4? or 2.Kd4? lets the black king return in front of the pawn.
step.d_opposition.m3: It comes back in front of the pawn, on c8.
step.d_opposition.m4: 3.Kc6! Face to face again, now on the sixth rank. Only this move and 3.c5 win.
step.d_opposition.m5: With no square in front of my king, it gives way again.
step.d_opposition.m6: 4.Kd7: my king takes c7 and c8, the pawn's road.
step.d_opposition.m7: The black king has no way back in front of the pawn.
step.d_opposition.m8: Now the pawn walks to c8 on its own, with my king beside it.
step.t_diagonal: Your king is on a1, far from the pawn, and the black king is already close. Does the pawn run on its own? If not, which way does your king get there in time to win?
step.t_diagonal.hint1: First the square: from e3 to e8. The black king is already inside.
step.t_diagonal.hint2: Your king must stand in front of the pawn, on d4, e4 or f4, before the black king gets there.
step.t_diagonal.hint3: Count the moves along both roads. Along the diagonal, the king gains a file and a rank with every move.
step.diagonal: In part 2 my king was already in front of the pawn. And when it is far away? The black king is inside the square, so the pawn waits: if it moves now, the black king catches it. Now the king's ruler: from a1 to d4 is three moves, the same three as from a1 to d1. On the diagonal the king moves sideways and forward at the same time.
step.d_diagonal: Count both kings' moves with me.
step.d_diagonal.m1: 1.Kb2!, along the diagonal. 1.Kb1? or 1.e4? let the black king get in front of the pawn first.
step.d_diagonal.m2: The black king also runs along the diagonal, heading for e4: the defender counts the moves the same way, and in part 6 you will be the one running.
step.d_diagonal.m3: 2.Kc3!, one more step along the long diagonal. 2.e4? would now only draw: the black king reaches the pawn before my king.
step.d_diagonal.m4: It takes e4 and e5, the squares in front of the pawn.
step.d_diagonal.m5: 3.Kd4! My king is next to the pawn and protects e3. The black king can no longer take it.
step.d_diagonal.m6: The black king stands in front of the pawn.
step.d_diagonal.m7: 4.Ke4!, the opposition from part 2, now on the fourth rank; it is the only winning move. From here it is the technique you've already seen.
step.diagonalMove: White to play and win. The pawn on f2 cannot run on its own. Take your king in front of it.
step.diagonalMove.hint: Along the diagonal, towards e4. 1.f3 or 1.f4 now let the black king catch the pawn.
step.diagonalMove.done: 3.Ke4, in front of the pawn and ahead of the black king. Three moves along the diagonal, and the pawn didn't even have to move.
step.t_defOpp: The white king wants to climb in front of the pawn. Where does your king stop it, to hold the draw?
step.t_defOpp.hint1: Think about the white king, not the pawn.
step.t_defOpp.hint2: Stepping back looks safe, but then the white king is the one facing you.
step.defendOpp: So far you attacked. Now switch sides: the opposition works for both. 1...Kd5! puts the kings face to face with one square between them, and the white king is the one that must give way. 1...Kd7? steps back and lets the white king take the opposition with 2.Kd4; from there it gets through, as in part 2.
step.d_defOpp: Watch how the black king shadows the white king.
step.d_defOpp.m1: 1...Kd5! Face to face with the white king, and d4 is under my control.
step.d_defOpp.m2: The white king tries to go round the side.
step.d_defOpp.m3: 2...Ke5! I follow it and stand face to face again. It is the only drawing move.
step.d_defOpp.m4: The pawn advances with check, to push my king out of the way.
step.d_defOpp.m5: I go back in front of the pawn: d5 is mine, and the white king can't climb through it.
step.d_defOpp.m6: The white king goes back behind the pawn.
step.d_defOpp.m7: I step back on the same file, still in front of the pawn. When the white king climbs, I stand face to face with it again: the same opposition.
step.defOppMove: Black to play and draw. The white king is in front of the pawn. Take the opposition.
step.defOppMove.hint: In front of the white king, one square between you. 1...Kc6? or 1...Kb6? step back and lose.
step.defOppMove.done: That's it. Each time the white king goes to the side, you go with it.
step.t_front: The black pawn is on d3 and its king, on f3, is coming to help it. Where must your king stand to hold the draw?
step.t_front.hint1: The square that matters is d1, where the pawn queens.
step.t_front.hint2: Beside the pawn is not enough: the pawn gets past.
step.defendFront: In part 4 the attacking king was in front of the pawn. Now the black king is already beside it. This position is from Matanović's Encyclopedia of Chess Endings, and it carries three rules: stay in front of the pawn; when the pawn advances, step straight back; when the black king comes to the side, stand face to face with it.
step.d_matanovic: Black to move. Follow the three rules, move by move.
step.d_matanovic.m1: The black king moves away, to try to get in through e2.
step.d_matanovic.m2: 2.Kd2!, in front of the pawn; 2.Kd1 also holds. 2.Kf1? loses, because it stands beside the pawn and the pawn gets past.
step.d_matanovic.m3: It comes back to push the pawn to d2.
step.d_matanovic.m4: 3.Kd1! Straight back. 3.Ke1? and 3.Kc1? lose: the black king gets into d2 or e2.
step.d_matanovic.m5: The black king comes to the side of the pawn.
step.d_matanovic.m6: 4.Ke1! Face to face with it, one square between us. It is the only move that holds.
step.d_matanovic.m7: The pawn advances with check, and my king has to leave e1.
step.d_matanovic.m8: 5.Kd1!, in front of the pawn again.
step.d_matanovic.m9: To protect the pawn, the black king takes my king's last square, and I am not in check: stalemate. A draw.
step.frontMove: White to play and draw. Now the pawn is on the c-file.
step.frontMove.hint: In front of the pawn; when the black king comes to the side, face to face with it.
step.frontMove.done: If the black king goes to c3 to protect the pawn, it is stalemate; if it leaves, you take the pawn.
step.t_seventh: The pawn is two squares from queening, and the black king stands in front of it. Only one move wins: which one, and why not the others?
step.t_seventh.hint1: Your king is already on the sixth, next to the pawn.
step.t_seventh.hint2: After the advance, can the black king still stand in front of the pawn?
step.seventh: In part 5 you stalemated the attacking king, and in part 6 you ran with the defending king. Now you attack again: how not to fall for it. The rule of thumb: with the king on the sixth, the pawn goes to the seventh without giving check. 1.c7 takes away the square in front from the black king, and it has to leave (only 1...Kb7). If the pawn gave check, the black king would step in front of it, and my king could only protect the pawn by stalemating. With a knight pawn and the black king in the corner, count its squares before every move: the check that looks strong can stalemate.
step.d_seventh: The advance without check, move by move.
step.d_seventh.m1: 1.c7!, without check: b8 and d8 are covered by the pawn, and the black king has to leave the square in front.
step.d_seventh.m2: It is the black king's only move, and now it stands beside the pawn, not in front of it.
step.d_seventh.m3: 2.Kd7! I protect c8. 2.c8=Q+? now would be taken with 2...Kxc8.
step.d_seventh.m4: Nothing to be done: c8 is mine, and the black king can't reach the pawn.
step.d_seventh.m5: A new queen, and the rest is the king and queen mate.
step.d_check: Now the mistake. With the black king on d8, 1.c7+? gives check. See what the black king does.
step.d_check.m1: 1...Kc8! The king steps in front of the pawn. 1...Ke8? would lose: 2.c8=Q+, and the black king can't reach the queen.
step.d_check.m2: To keep protecting the pawn, the white king goes to c6, and the black king has no move and no check: stalemate.
step.knightMove: White to play and win. A knight pawn, the black king in the corner. Before each move, count its squares.
step.knightMove.hint: 1.b6?? leaves the black king with no square and no check.
step.knightMove.done: The pawn queens with check on b8. With a knight pawn, the corner is the defender's weapon, and you counted the squares in time.
step.t_barcza: Zurich, 1959: Barcza, with White, against the young Fischer. After a long rook ending, both sides queened; in the queen ending, Fischer took the a4 pawn and the queens came off. Black's rook pawn was left. Only one move draws. Where does your king go?
step.t_barcza.hint1: Against a rook pawn, the defender only needs to reach the corner.
step.t_barcza.hint2: The corner is a1. The black king wants to shut the road on b2 and b3. Count the moves to c1.
step.barcza: In part 7 the corner was a trap for the attacker; now it is your defence. The game ended here, drawn, without another move: Barcza had the draw in hand. With 96.Kd2! and 97.Kc1! the white king reaches the corner before the black king can shut the door on b2. On a1 nobody can drive it out; the black king can only box it in by stalemating it.
step.d_barcza: The road that holds, move by move.
step.d_barcza.m1: 96.Kd2!, heading for c1 along the diagonal. 96.Ke2? or 96.Kd3? arrive too late.
step.d_barcza.m2: The black king tries to shut the road on b2.
step.d_barcza.m3: 97.Kc1! Now b1 and b2 are within my reach.
step.d_barcza.m4: With no way to drive my king out, the pawn advances.
step.d_barcza.m5: 98.Kb1!, closer to the corner. 98.Kd1? or 98.Kd2? lose: the black king gets into b2 and the pawn queens.
step.d_barcza.m6: The pawn reaches the third rank.
step.d_barcza.m7: 99.Ka1!, into the corner; it is the only move that holds.
step.d_barcza.m8: My king has no square and is not in check: stalemate. A draw.
step.cornerMove: Black to play and draw. A knight pawn, and the white king beside it. Which corner?
step.cornerMove.hint: 1...Kb8? looks like the square in front, but 2.b7! takes the pawn to the seventh without check, the rule from part 7.
step.cornerMove.done: Now, to keep protecting the pawn, the white king has to go to b6, and it is stalemate.
key.matanovic: The defender stays in front of the pawn: step straight back and stand face to face with the other king. Draw.
key.barcza: Barcza against Fischer, Zurich, 1959: only Fischer's rook pawn is left, and the white king runs to the corner in time. Draw.
part.defendRace.title: The defender runs along the diagonal too
part.defendRace.summary: Your king far from the pawn: count both kings' moves and get in front along the diagonal.
step.t_defRace: The white king is coming to help the pawn, and your king is on the other side of the board. Only one road arrives in time. Where does your king go, to hold the draw?
step.t_defRace.hint1: First the square: from c4 to c8. Your king is inside, so the pawn can't run on its own: the race is between the kings.
step.t_defRace.hint2: The white king wants b5, beside the pawn; yours wants c6, in front of it. Count each king's moves.
step.t_defRace.hint3: From f4 to c6 is three moves, but only if every move gains a file and a rank at once. What is the first square on that road?
step.defRace: In parts 4 and 5 your king was already near the pawn. Now it is far away, and the ruler from part 3 works for the defender too: count both kings' moves. The white king needs three moves to reach b5, beside the pawn: its own pawn blocks its diagonal on c4. Yours needs three to reach c6, in front of the pawn, and the only three-move road runs through e5 and d6: along the diagonal. 1...Kf5? gains only a rank, costs one move more, and the white king gets there first.
step.d_defRace: The race between the two kings, move by move.
step.d_defRace.m1: 1...Ke5! A file and a rank at once, heading for d6. 1...Kf5? reaches d6 one move later, and loses.
step.d_defRace.m2: 2.Kc3, the shortest road to b4 and b5.
step.d_defRace.m3: 2...Kd6! One more step along the diagonal: c6 and c7 are now within my reach.
step.d_defRace.m5: 3...Kc6! In front of the pawn, and b5 is closed to the white king. It is the only drawing move: 3...Kc7? allows 4.Kb5, and it gets through.
step.d_defRace.m6: 4.Ka5: it tries to go round on the a-file.
step.d_defRace.m7: 4...Kc7. I let the white king climb and wait for it: when it comes to b5, I stand face to face. 4...Kc5, attacking the pawn, also draws.
step.d_defRace.m9: 5...Kb7! The opposition from part 4: it is the white king's move, and it has to give way. If the pawn advances, I step straight back, as in part 5.
step.defRaceMove: Black to play and draw. Now the pawn is on the e-file, and your king is far away. Get in front of it before the white king does.
step.defRaceMove.hint: Along the diagonal, towards the front of the pawn: every move gains a file and a rank. The straight move arrives one move late.
step.defRaceMove.done: 3...Ke6, in front of the pawn and before the white king reaches d5. If 4.e5, 4...Ke7! and, after 5.Kd5, 5...Kd7: the opposition.
